samasa.sense: by her terrifying peals of laughter

samasa.alt: शिवदूती could be a separate nominative (‘Śivadūtī …’), but then अभिदूषिताः has no agent and सा in the second line repeats her; the compound fits better.

morph.note: Perfect of √खाद्, reduplicated च-खाद (kh → c in the reduplication).
अभिदूषित: अभि + causative of √दुष् (दूषय-) + क्त, ‘spoiled, harmed, assailed’. Here: overwhelmed by the laughter.

mantras.anvaya: शिवदूत्यभिदूषिताः असुराः चण्डाट्टहासैः पृथिव्यां पेतुः; अथ तदा सा पतितान् तान् चखाद।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the asuras fell; then she devoured them.
mantras.lit: The asuras, assailed by Śivadūtī with fierce loud laughs, fell on the earth; and then she at that time devoured them as they lay fallen.
mantras.tr: Struck down by Śivadūtī’s fierce peals of laughter, the asuras fell to the ground, and there she devoured them.

comm.t: Śivadūtī is the power that came out of Caṇḍikā’s own body with the cry of a hundred jackals (8.23) and sent Śiva as her messenger (8.28). Her weapon is her laughter: it fells the asuras, and she eats the fallen.
The same terrible laughter returns in the next battle (9.23 अट्टाट्टहासमशिवं शिवदूती चकार ह), and the hymn of chapter 11 salutes her as Śivadūtī who slew the mighty Daityas (11.20).

sandhi.note: ā + a → ā; then three visargas after ai, ai and u are each sounded r before a voiced consonant (v, n, d).

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (देवारि)
samasa.literal: the soldiers of the enemies of the gods
samasa.sense: the rank and file of the asura army

morph.note: Perfect of √नश्, formed like पेतुः (8.35) with e and no reduplicated syllable. √नश् means both ‘perish’ and ‘be lost, vanish’; with 8.40 (‘seeing the Daityas intent on flight’) the sense is ‘they made off, disappeared’.
Present participle of the causative stem मर्दय- of √मृद् ‘crush’, accusative singular agreeing with the collective मातृगणम्.

mantras.anvaya: इति क्रुद्धं महासुरान् मर्दयन्तं मातृगणं दृष्ट्वा देवारिसैनिकाः विविधैः अभ्युपायैः नेशुः।
mantras.lit: Seeing thus the band of Mothers, enraged, crushing the great asuras, the soldiers of the gods’ enemies vanished by various means.
mantras.tr: When they saw the furious band of Mothers crushing the great asuras, the soldiers of the gods’ enemies slipped away, each however he could.
mantras.tr_note: नेशुः is taken as ‘vanished, fled’ (see morph); ‘each however he could’ renders अभ्युपायैर्विविधैः.

comm.t: The rout of the common soldiers. The word for the Mothers is now collective — मातृगण, ‘the band of Mothers’ — and the asura rank and file disappear, as they will again in 9.41 (केचिद्विनेशुरसुराः केचिन्नष्टा महाहवात्).

flags.uncertain: नेशुः may also be rendered ‘perished (in various ways)’. The next verse speaks of the Daityas as ‘intent on flight’, so ‘vanished, fled’ is preferred.

morph.note: Perfect of √या (ययौ) with two prefixes: अभि + आ + ययौ → अभ्याययौ (अभि’s i becomes y before आ, इको यणचि 6.1.77). The same verb brought the Mothers to the field (8.17 अभ्याययौ).

mantras.anvaya: मातृगणार्दितान् दैत्यान् पलायनपरान् दृष्ट्वा क्रुद्धः रक्तबीजः महासुरः योद्धुम् अभ्याययौ।
mantras.lit: Seeing the Daityas, harried by the band of Mothers, intent on flight, the great asura Raktabīja, enraged, came forward to fight.
mantras.tr: When he saw the Daityas, harried by the Mothers, turning to flee, the great asura Raktabīja advanced in fury to fight.

comm.t: Raktabīja enters, and the chapter takes its name from him (रक्तबीजवधः). His name is explained by the verse that follows: his blood is seed.

samasa.vigraha: तस्य प्रमाणम् इव प्रमाणं यस्य सः
samasa.sense: as big and as strong as Raktabīja himself

morph.note: Present tense for a standing fact: ‘whenever a drop falls, an asura springs up’. The narrative pauses to state the rule of his nature.
The taddhita -तस् gives an indeclinable with ablative meaning: शरीरतः = शरीरात्, ‘from the body’.

mantras.anvaya: यदा अस्य शरीरतः रक्तबिन्दुः भूमौ पतति, तदा मेदिन्यां तत्प्रमाणः असुरः समुत्पतति।
mantras.anvaya_en: A यदा … तदा sentence in the present: condition and consequence.
mantras.lit: Whenever a drop of blood falls from his body to the ground, then an asura of his size springs up on the earth.
mantras.tr: Whenever a drop of his blood fell to the ground, an asura of his own stature sprang up from the earth.
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit present of general truth is rendered as a past, to keep the narrative tense.

comm.t: The verse states Raktabīja’s peculiar power: every drop of blood that reaches the earth becomes another asura his equal. The Devī Māhātmya gives the rule without explaining where it came from.

A modern reading: violence that only spills more of what it attacks multiplies it. The episode is often read today as a picture of habits and desires that grow each time they are fought on their own terms.

flags.uncertain: Variant (corrections.json): for the Gita Press तत्प्रमाणस्तदासुरः, GRETIL and Freund read तत्प्रमाणो महासुरः (‘a great asura of his size’). The Gita Press reading is kept; the sense is the same, only तदा (the correlative of यदा) is replaced by महा-.

samasa.sense: with Aindrī, named in the next line

samasa.literal: with the thunderbolt of her own

morph.note: Perfect of √युध् in the ātmanepada, as the root requires: reduplicated यु-युध्-, ending -ए. Contrast the parasmaipada युयुधुः in 8.45.

mantras.anvaya: सः गदापाणिः महासुरः इन्द्रशक्त्या (सह) युयुधे; ततः च ऐन्द्री स्ववज्रेण रक्तबीजम् अताडयत्।
mantras.lit: He, the great asura, mace in hand, fought with the power of Indra; and then Aindrī struck Raktabīja with her own thunderbolt.
mantras.tr: Mace in hand, the great asura fought with Indra’s power, and Aindrī struck Raktabīja with her thunderbolt.

comm.t: Raktabīja’s first opponent is Aindrī. Her blow with the vajra draws the first blood, and the next verse shows what it produces.
